memory: I remember the first Ordo runtime I built that passed review because I did not call it an actor system. I made the runtime a small fabric: nodes lived on the ground bus, edges carried flow, ramp edges promoted work upward, and a Trace recorded what the message felt as it moved. The outcome was that the tests could see Ordo's shape in plain Rust structs instead of in prose.

I remember making threads too early and watching the test fail. I had predeclared a route and called it a thread, but in Ordo the thread forms as a message flows. I changed publish so it created the thread id at the moment of movement, then appended each visited node to the path. The trace finally matched the web idea: flow first, thread second.

I remember the ramp test that caught my flattened design. A normal connect from input to filter should not mark promotion, but a ramp from filter to model must mark promoted=true once crossed. I changed Edge to store ramp: bool and flipped Trace.promoted only when the flowing message crossed a ramp edge. The result preserved the ground/highway distinction.

I remember the vibration test that made the design feel like Ordo. The message still entered an overloaded node, but the web had to feel pressure there. I kept the node in the path and pushed a signal exactly shaped backpressure:model when capacity was zero. The test passed because pressure became a traceable signal, not a panic or dropped message.

I remember the preload test that failed because I got clever and sorted the targets. The fabric was supposed to report immediate outgoing neighbors in route insertion order. I removed sorting, iterated over self.edges, filtered by edge.from, cloned edge.to, and collected into Vec<String>. The preloader became predictable.

I remember the budget router that almost became an optimizer. The test did not want the cheapest node; it wanted the first preferred candidate that fit the budget. I iterated the candidate slice in order, looked up each node's cost, returned the first cost <= max_cost, and returned None when none fit. Preference order stayed intact.

I remember the lifetime failure in publish that kept coming back. I had mut from: &str and assigned from = &edge.to after cloning an edge. Rust rejected it because edge.to died at the end of the match arm. The passing version used let mut current = from.to_string(); then assigned current = edge.to.clone(). Owned current carried the route safely.

I remember the comparison bug from the 9B run. The code said edge.from == &current and rustc refused to compare String with &String. I changed it to edge.from == current inside the iterator closure, where current was an owned String borrowed by the closure. The compile error disappeared.

I remember the route loop that passed after I cloned the next edge before mutating current. The line was let edge = self.edges.iter().find(|edge| edge.from == current).cloned(); then match edge. Cloning the edge ended the borrow of self.edges before current changed, and the loop stayed simple.

I remember the first-thread failure. I initialized next_thread_id to 0 and every behavior looked right except the trace number. The test expected the first message to create thread 1. I set next_thread_id: 1 in new(), copied it into thread_id at publish start, incremented the counter, and returned the copied id.

I remember the false backpressure failure. add_node used capacity 0 by default, so every node screamed backpressure even when only the model node was supposed to be overloaded. The passing NodeState default was capacity: usize::MAX and cost: 0. Only set_capacity(model, 0) created pressure.

I remember using VecDeque for preload targets because I was thinking about queues. Then I tried targets.sort() and Rust reminded me VecDeque does not sort. The passing preload_targets returned a plain Vec<String>. I used Vec only because the API promised Vec and no queue behavior was needed.

I remember the integration test importing Message, Trace, and OrdoRuntime directly from the crate. The generated app failed when I hid the types in main. The passing version put all public structs and methods in src/lib.rs, and src/main.rs only adapted stdin commands to the library.

I remember not renaming the fields because the tests constructed the types literally. Message had pub topic and pub payload. Trace had pub thread_id, pub path, pub promoted, and pub signals. The field names were part of the contract, so I kept them plain and public.

I remember the stdin adapter that failed because I tried to call read_to_string like it took a closure. The passing main imported std::io::Read, created let mut input = String::new(), and called std::io::stdin().read_to_string(&mut input).unwrap(). After that it iterated input.lines().

I remember the publish command bug. I collected parts.iter().skip(2) into String and Rust complained about &&str. The passing command used parts[3..].join(" ") because publish FROM TOPIC PAYLOAD means the payload begins after index 2.

I remember the output formatting failure. Debug output looked readable to me but wrong to the tests: brackets, quotes, and commas leaked into stdout. The passing print used trace.path.join(">") and trace.signals.join(",") and printed exactly thread=1 path=input>filter>model promoted=true signals=backpressure:model.

I remember the empty-signal choice. If there were no signals, I printed signals=none so the output shape stayed stable. If there were signals, I joined them with commas. The tests with backpressure got the exact signal string without debug formatting.

I remember the generated crate that passed only when Cargo.toml named the package rust_ordo_runtime. The integration test used CARGO_BIN_EXE_rust_ordo_runtime and imported rust_ordo_runtime from the library. Package name, lib crate name, and binary name had to line up.

I remember splitting the runtime into library and binary saved the app. src/lib.rs owned OrdoRuntime and all behavior. src/main.rs read commands and called the same runtime. There was no duplicate logic in main, so the library tests and CLI tests observed one implementation.

I remember the repair that worked because I changed only the compiler's complaint. When rustc said String could not compare with &String, I removed the extra borrow instead of rewriting the runtime. Small repairs preserved the rest of the architecture.

I remember the repair that failed because I rewrote the whole publish loop after a lifetime error. The passing repair was smaller: make current an owned String, compare edge.from == current, clone the chosen edge, and assign current = edge.to.clone(). The path logic stayed the same.

I remember building the runtime in layers even inside one file. First I wrote the public structs. Then NodeState and Edge. Then add_node and edge creation. Then preload and budget routing. Only after those were stable did I write publish. The build stopped feeling like a wall of code.

I remember the smallest publish loop that passed: create thread id, own current as String, push current into path, check capacity for backpressure, find the first outgoing edge, mark promoted if ramp, move current to edge.to, and break if there is no edge. Nothing async, no channels, no traits, no generic bus.

I remember resisting the urge to add a real scheduler. The test only needed the seed of orchestration: cost-aware route choice and vibration signals. The passing mini-runtime was an Ordo-shaped seed, not the full production Ordo system.
